claims.claim: Procopius of Gaza was a Christian sophist and rhetorician, one of the most important representatives of the Rhetorical School of Gaza, born roughly in 465–470 and died approximately 526–530.
Procopius of Gaza was a rhetorician and biblical exegete, perhaps the foremost figure of the 'School of Gaza', a group of Christian rhetoricians of the 5th–6th century.
Procopius of Gaza was the preceptor of Choricius the sophist and lived during the time of Justin and Justinian (518–565).

The Refutation of Proclus' Elements of Theology (Ἀνάπτυξις τῆς Θεολογικῆς Στοιχειώσεως Πρόκλου τοῦ Λυκίου = Refutatio Procli) attributed to the twelfth-century Byzantine theologian Nicholas of Methone (died between 1160–1166) is an important witness to the circulation and reception of Proclus' work in eleventh- and twelfth-century Byzantium.

The paternity of the Refutatio Procli has stirred controversy as two fourteenth-century Vatican manuscripts ascribe two of the many sections composing this work to the late antique rhetor and theologian Procopius of Gaza (ca. 465/470–526/530 CE).
The dispute about authorship appeared to be settled in 1984 with the publication of the editio princeps of Nicholas of Methone's work.
Eugenio Amato has defended the Procopian authorship of the text, editing the two sections of the Refutatio Procli ascribed to Procopius as authentic Procopian fragments.
According to Amato, Nicholas of Methone appropriated an earlier Procopian work for purely rhetorical purposes and without declaring his source.
The surviving fragment of Procopius' Refutatio Procli comes from codex Vaticanus graecus 1096 and contains the refutation of chapter 140 (ρμ΄) of Proclus' Theological Chapters.

Modern scholarship rejects the Procopian authorship of several occasional pieces and assigns to Nicholas of Methone (12th century) the polemical treatise against the Neoplatonism of Proclus, an example of Byzantine pseudepigraphy.
